entities.name: Lê Nghi Dân
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Lê Nghi Dân (黎宜民), known as Marquis Lệ Đức, briefly held the throne as the fourth Emperor of the Lê dynasty of Đại Việt during a tumultuous period in 15th-century Southeast Asian history. His eight-month reign, from October 1459 to June 1460, marked a significant disruption in the imperial succession, highlighting the simmering power struggles within the court following the death of Emperor Lê Thái Tông. Born the eldest son of Lê Thái Tông, his ascension was controversial, rooted in a coup d'état against his younger half-brother, the child emperor Lê Nhân Tông, and his regent mother, Empress Nguyễn Thị Anh. This episode underscores the fragility of imperial authority and the potent influence of court factions in shaping dynastic fortunes in pre-modern Đại Việt.

Lê Nghi Dân seized power in October 1459 by orchestrating a coup that resulted in the assassination of Emperor Lê Nhân Tông and Empress Nguyễn Thị Anh. His brief tenure was characterized by attempts to consolidate his authority and reward his supporters. He issued decrees promoting officials who aided his ascent and sought to legitimize his rule by claiming the throne as the rightful eldest son. However, his actions were perceived as illegitimate by a powerful coalition of court officials, including Nguyễn Xí and Đinh Liệt, who remained loyal to the established order and viewed his seizure of power as an affront to dynastic stability and Confucian principles of succession.

His actions highlighted deep-seated power struggles within the Lê dynasty, shaping future succession protocols.

entities.summary:
Lê Nghi Dân, born Lê Nghi Dân (黎宜民) in Hanoi on October 1, 1439, briefly ascended to the throne of Đại Việt as the fourth Emperor of the Lê dynasty, marking a period of significant political upheaval in the mid-15th century. As the eldest son of Emperor Lê Thái Tông, he was initially designated heir but was later demoted to Marquis of Lệ Đức following his mother's disgrace. Despite this demotion, his familial connection to the imperial line positioned him as a potential claimant amidst the growing discontent with his younger half-brother, Emperor Lê Nhân Tông, and the regency of Empress Nguyễn Thị Anh.

His rise to power was orchestrated through a dramatic coup d'état in October 1459. Exploiting the vulnerabilities of the young Emperor Lê Nhân Tông and his regent, Lê Nghi Dân seized the capital, Thăng Long, and ordered the assassination of both Nhân Tông and Nguyễn Thị Anh. His reign, though short-lived at merely eight months, saw him attempt to consolidate power by promoting his supporters and issuing some decrees, yet he struggled to gain the full legitimacy and respect of the established court and powerful mandarins. His rule was characterized by the violent nature of his ascension and the subsequent instability it generated within the imperial court, undermining the traditional order of succession.
